question: An early-stage Indian SaaS company has ₹200cr ARR, 120% NRR, but negative EBITDA of -₹50cr. Which valuation metric is most appropriate?
before: PE and EV/EBITDA are meaningless with negative earnings/EBITDA. P/BV is irrelevant for SaaS whose value lies in customer relationships, not balance sheet. EV/ARR values the recurring revenue base — the core asset. 120% NRR is very positive (existing customers spending 20% more each year).
after:
Concept: Valuation metric selection depends on the company's financial stage and what drives value. Early-stage SaaS companies with recurring revenue but negative profitability require metrics that value the revenue base itself, not accounting earnings.

Why this is correct: EV/ARR (Enterprise Value divided by Annual Recurring Revenue) is the only metric that values the company on its recurring revenue stream, which is the core asset of a SaaS business. The 120% NRR demonstrates strong unit economics and customer retention — existing customers are expanding spend by 20% annually — signaling that the revenue base will grow and eventually become profitable. This metric directly reflects the intrinsic value of the subscription business model.

Why the others are wrong:

A) PE ratio — PE divides price by net income (earnings). With negative EBITDA of -₹50cr, the company has negative or near-zero net income, making this ratio meaningless or negative. PE cannot be applied to unprofitable companies.

B) EV/EBITDA — This metric requires positive EBITDA to be interpretable. With -₹50cr EBITDA, the multiple is negative or undefined. EBITDA-based valuation is designed for mature, cash-generative businesses, not early-stage SaaS.

C) Price-to-Book Value — P/BV values a company based on net asset value on the balance sheet. SaaS companies derive value from intangible customer relationships, brand, and recurring revenue contracts — not tangible assets. The balance sheet understates true value, making P/BV irrelevant and misleading.

Intuition: Early-stage SaaS investors focus on revenue growth, unit economics (NRR and CAC payback), and path to profitability, not current earnings. A 120% NRR in a ₹200cr ARR company signals strong product-market fit and self-expanding value — the metric must capture future cash generation potential, not past profitability. This is why venture-backed and high-growth SaaS are valued on revenue multiples, not earnings.
